processing: Typically a lightly oxidised, rolled Anxi oolong, made in the same way as light Tie Guan Yin. The label describes style and grade, not a harvest method.
harvest_season: As with other Anxi oolongs, spring and autumn; sellers usually state the year.
appearance_dry: Tight, green rolled pellets like those of light Tie Guan Yin, as usual for the style.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green and clear, typical of light Anxi oolong.
appearance_wet: Whole green leaves open out, as with light Tie Guan Yin.
taste_profile: Expect what light Anxi Tie Guan Yin usually gives: floral, soft and creamy, with a sweet finish. Quality varies widely because the name is not tied to one standard.

brewing.notes: Brew it as a light Tie Guan Yin: very hot water, a quick rinse to open the pellets and short first steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like other Anxi oolongs, and shop listings commonly name the year. The light style is best within about a year of picking. There is no regulated grade behind the label, so the name itself tells you nothing about the season or the quality.
description:
Monkey Picked is a trade name, not a harvest method. It usually means an Anxi oolong made from the Tieguanyin variety, sold as a higher grade, and its Cantonese form ma liu mie simply says monkey-plucked.

Nothing about the processing sets it apart: as with light Tie Guan Yin, the leaf is lightly oxidised and rolled into pellets. Any difference you taste comes from the particular lot, not from a separate method.

In the cup, then, think of light Tie Guan Yin, with florals and a creamy body. Use very hot water and short steeps, and judge the tea by how it lasts over several infusions.

Buy with care. The name once suggested something rare, but it now covers a wide range of grades, including cheap ones, and it is not protected. Compare it with a Tie Guan Yin of known season before paying extra, and ignore any claim about real monkeys.
history:
Legends about it vary. Monkeys are said to have been trained, by farmers or monks, to reach wild trees on Fujian cliffs, and some versions move the story to the Wuyi Mountains. Other tellings admit that merchants made the story up. No historical evidence supports any working monkey harvest.

The Cantonese name suggests Hong Kong or southern Chinese trade use, and one account credits mid-twentieth-century Hong Kong merchants with coining it, though this is hard to confirm. Over time the label moved from implying rarity to a broad commercial style.
